title: This week in 5 numbers: Nearly 4 in 10 workers don’t trust HR to help in toxic situations
summary: Here’s a roundup of numbers from the last week — including how many workers were targeted in job scam attempts.

title: DC Water to pay roughly $217,000 to settle claim it replaced HR worker with younger employee
summary: The District of Columbia Water and Sewer Authority must also enhance its nondiscrimination policies and provide advanced antidiscrimination training.

title: Men outearn women by more than $12K annually, data shows
summary: “As more women joined the full-time workforce, the per-worker difference compounded into a much larger estimated overall gap,” a career expert said.

title: On its 60th birthday, SHRM’s nonprofit arm pushes for better caregiver support
summary: Employers can’t reliably address working caregivers’ needs through policies and employee benefits alone, said Wendi Safstrom, president of the SHRM Foundation.

title: WorkSmart settles EEOC claim it failed to hire, refer women per a client request
summary: Staffing agencies have repeatedly drawn the agency’s attention for allegedly discriminating based on protected characteristics to satisfy the demands of a client.

title: Nearly 7 in 10 workers say they didn’t get a raise in the past 6 months
summary: Increased transparency about pay and workforce decisions can improve the perception gap between employers and employees, Morgan McKinley found.

title: PIP’s proximity to plaintiff’s EEOC charge can’t save bias complaint, 3rd Circuit says
summary: A Black former BNY employee failed to show that his placement on a performance improvement plan was the result of race-based discrimination.

title: Edward Jones pushes back on lawsuit challenging diversity program
summary: The employer critiqued the plaintiff’s attempt to form a class of “all White” advisors while simultaneously alleging White women benefited from the program.

title: US labor market continues to be ‘low hire, low fire’
summary: Current trends indicate slower job growth ahead as an increasing number of consumers say they’re having trouble finding jobs.

title: CEOs fear they’re underinvesting in AI
summary: More than half of chief executives are concerned their businesses will fall behind due to limitations in technology foundations, according to a new survey.
